name: Battle of Thermopylae
sides: Greek city-states led by Sparta vs the Achaemenid Persian Empire
commanders: King Leonidas I of Sparta vs King Xerxes I
forces: About 7,000 Greeks vs perhaps 100,000–150,000 Persians (Herodotus claimed millions)
casualties: Nearly all of the last 1,500 Greeks killed, including the 300 Spartans; Persian losses estimated at up to 20,000
summary: A small Greek army held the narrow coastal pass of Thermopylae for three days against Xerxes' invasion, until a local man showed the Persians a mountain path around them.
tactics: The pass, only about 15 m wide in places between cliffs and sea, cancelled out Persian numbers and cavalry. Greek hoplites in a tight phalanx, with long spears and big bronze shields, rotated units so tired men could rest, and repeatedly beat back waves of Persians, including the elite Immortals. A Greek fleet at Artemisium simultaneously blocked the Persians from sailing around.
betrayal: A Greek from Trachis named Ephialtes, hoping for a reward, guided the Persian Immortals along the Anopaea mountain path at night to get behind the Greeks. His name came to mean 'nightmare' in Greek. Knowing they were surrounded, Leonidas sent most of the army away and stayed with the 300 Spartans, 700 Thespians and 400 Thebans (who surrendered).
atrocities: Xerxes reportedly ordered Leonidas's body to be beheaded and crucified, an outrage against Greek custom. The Persians then burned Athens and the Acropolis temples.
reshaped: Though a defeat, the stand bought time and became a symbol of resistance. Weeks later the Greek fleet won at Salamis and then the army at Plataea (479 BCE), ending Persia's attempt to conquer Greece and allowing the Athenian golden age of democracy and philosophy.
connections: Persian Wars; Classical Greece; Achaemenid Persian Empire; Darius I; Herodotus

name: Battle of Cannae
sides: Carthage vs the Roman Republic
commanders: Hannibal Barca vs consuls Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Gaius Terentius Varro
forces: About 50,000 Carthaginians and allies vs about 86,000 Romans
casualties: About 50,000–70,000 Romans killed in a single afternoon — one of the bloodiest days in history; about 6,000 Carthaginians
summary: Hannibal annihilated the largest army Rome had ever fielded with a double envelopment, still studied in military academies.
tactics: Hannibal placed his weaker Gallic and Spanish infantry in a forward-bulging crescent at the centre and his best African infantry on the flanks. As the Romans pushed back the centre, they were drawn into a pocket; the African infantry turned inward, and Carthaginian cavalry, having routed the Roman horse, attacked from behind. Surrounded and packed so tightly they could not swing their swords, the Romans were slaughtered.
betrayal: After Cannae many southern Italian allies, including Capua, defected to Hannibal. Yet most of Rome's Latin allies stayed loyal, which ultimately saved Rome.
atrocities: Survivors were sold into slavery; legend says Hannibal sent a bushel of gold rings from dead Roman nobles to Carthage. Rome performed human sacrifices — burying two Gauls and two Greeks alive in the Forum — in panic.
reshaped: Rome refused to surrender, adopted Fabius's strategy of avoiding battle, and eventually invaded Africa; Scipio defeated Hannibal at Zama (202 BCE). Cannae became the model 'battle of annihilation' studied by later generals, including German planners in 1914.
connections: Punic Wars; Hannibal; Carthage; Roman Republic

name: Battle of the Teutoburg Forest
sides: Germanic tribes vs the Roman Empire
commanders: Arminius vs Publius Quinctilius Varus
forces: About 15,000–20,000 Romans in three legions
casualties: Almost all Romans killed or enslaved
summary: Three Roman legions were ambushed and destroyed over three days in forest and marsh — Rome's worst defeat under Augustus.
tactics: Arminius lured the Roman column, stretched out for kilometres, onto a narrow path between hill and bog in pouring rain. Germanic warriors attacked from behind a prepared earth wall, where legionaries could not form ranks.
betrayal: Arminius was a Cheruscan prince raised in Rome, a Roman citizen and an officer in the Roman army whom Varus trusted completely. He fed Varus false reports of a revolt to lead him into the trap; another chief, Segestes, warned Varus but was ignored.
atrocities: Captured officers were sacrificed to Germanic gods; Roman soldiers who found the site six years later saw skulls nailed to trees. Varus killed himself.
reshaped: Rome abandoned plans to conquer Germany beyond the Rhine, which became the long-term border between the Latin and Germanic worlds — shaping the languages and cultures of Europe.
connections: Teutoburg Forest; Roman Empire; Augustus; Julio-Claudian dynasty

name: Siege of Jerusalem (70 CE)
sides: Roman Empire vs Jewish rebels
commanders: Titus vs Simon bar Giora and John of Gischala
forces: About 60,000 Romans
casualties: Josephus claimed 1.1 million died (modern estimates far lower but still huge); 97,000 enslaved
summary: Rome crushed the Jewish revolt by besieging Jerusalem and destroying the Second Temple.
tactics: Titus surrounded the city with a siege wall to starve it, then used battering rams and siege towers to break three walls one by one, finally storming the Temple Mount.
betrayal: Inside, rival Jewish factions fought each other and burned food stores, worsening famine. The historian Josephus, a Jewish general who had surrendered, served Rome as negotiator and wrote the main account.
atrocities: Thousands of captives were crucified around the walls — up to 500 a day. Survivors were enslaved; some were forced to build the Colosseum, funded by Temple treasure.
reshaped: The destruction of the Temple ended sacrificial Judaism, which was reshaped into rabbinic Judaism centred on synagogues and study; Tisha B'Av still mourns it. The Arch of Titus shows the menorah being carried away.
connections: Judaism; Roman Empire; Colosseum; Ancient Israel and Judah

name: Siege of Masada
sides: Roman Empire vs Sicarii Jewish rebels
commanders: Lucius Flavius Silva vs Eleazar ben Ya'ir
forces: About 8,000 Romans vs 960 defenders
casualties: According to Josephus, 960 defenders died by mass suicide
summary: The last rebel stronghold on a desert mesa fell after the Romans built a gigantic siege ramp.
tactics: Herod's palace-fortress sat on a cliff 400 m high. Romans built a wall around it, then a ramp of earth and timber up the western side, rolled a siege tower up it and broke the wall.
atrocities: Josephus wrote that the defenders killed their families and themselves rather than be enslaved; historians debate his account.
reshaped: Masada became a symbol of resistance in modern Israel.
connections: Judaism; Roman Empire; Siege of Jerusalem (70 CE)

name: Battle of Kalinga
sides: Maurya Empire vs the Kalinga kingdom
commanders: Ashoka vs the people of Kalinga (ruler unknown)
forces: Unknown; Megasthenes credited Kalinga with 60,000 infantry, 1,000 cavalry and 700 elephants
casualties: 100,000 killed and 150,000 deported, by Ashoka's own Rock Edict XIII
summary: Ashoka's conquest of Kalinga was so bloody that it changed his life and the history of Buddhism.
tactics: Little is known; Mauryan armies used war elephants, cavalry and infantry on the coastal plain near the Daya river, which legend says ran red with blood.
atrocities: Ashoka himself recorded mass killing, deportation and the suffering of Brahmins, ascetics and ordinary families — a rare confession of a conqueror.
reshaped: Ashoka renounced conquest by war, embraced dhamma and sent Buddhist missionaries abroad, helping Buddhism become a world religion.

name: Battle of Karbala
sides: Umayyad Caliphate vs Husayn ibn Ali and his companions
commanders: Umar ibn Sa'd (for Caliph Yazid I) vs Husayn ibn Ali
forces: About 4,000 Umayyad soldiers vs about 72 companions and family
casualties: Husayn and nearly all his male companions killed, including his infant son Ali al-Asghar
summary: Husayn, grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, refused to pledge allegiance to Yazid and was killed with his small band — the defining tragedy of Shia Islam.
tactics: Husayn's party was surrounded on the plain and cut off from the Euphrates for days; on the tenth day they fought hopeless single combats and were overwhelmed.
betrayal: People of Kufa had sent Husayn thousands of letters inviting him to lead them against Yazid. When the Umayyad governor Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad terrorised the city and executed Husayn's envoy Muslim ibn Aqil, the Kufans abandoned him. Only a few, like the commander al-Hurr, switched to Husayn's side.
atrocities: Husayn's camp was denied water in desert heat; after the battle his head and those of his companions were carried on spears to Damascus, and the women and children, including his sister Zaynab, were taken captive.
reshaped: Karbala deepened the Sunni–Shia split; it is mourned every year on Ashura with processions across the world, including India, and became a lasting symbol of resistance to tyranny.
connections: Shia and Sunni split; Umayyad Caliphate; Islam; Prophet Muhammad

name: Battle of Hattin
sides: Ayyubid Sultanate vs the Kingdom of Jerusalem
commanders: Saladin vs King Guy of Lusignan and Raynald of Châtillon
forces: About 30,000 Ayyubids vs about 20,000 crusaders
casualties: Crusader army destroyed; most captured
summary: Saladin destroyed the crusader army after luring it into a waterless march in midsummer, leading to the fall of Jerusalem.
tactics: Saladin besieged Tiberias to draw the crusaders out. They marched through dry hills in July heat; Saladin's archers harassed them, blocked the springs, and set the brush on fire so smoke blew into their faces. Exhausted and thirsty, they were surrounded on the twin hills of Hattin.
betrayal: Bitter rivalry between Guy and Count Raymond of Tripoli split the crusader leadership; Raymond, who had advised against marching, broke through the lines and escaped, and was accused of treachery. Raynald had earlier broken a truce by attacking Muslim caravans and pilgrims.
atrocities: Saladin personally executed Raynald for his attacks on pilgrims and had about 200 captured Templar and Hospitaller knights beheaded; ordinary prisoners were sold as slaves. He spared King Guy.
reshaped: Jerusalem surrendered three months later. Europe launched the Third Crusade under Richard the Lionheart, which failed to retake the city.
connections: Saladin; Saladin retakes Jerusalem; Ayyubid dynasty; First Crusade; Christianity; Islam

name: Battle of Agincourt
sides: Kingdom of England vs Kingdom of France
commanders: Henry V vs Constable Charles d'Albret
forces: About 6,000–9,000 English, mostly longbowmen, vs about 12,000–15,000 French
casualties: About 6,000 French killed, many nobles; a few hundred English
summary: A sick, starving English army defeated a much larger French force in a muddy field — immortalised by Shakespeare's Henry V.
tactics: Heavy rain turned the newly ploughed field to mud between two woods. English longbowmen behind sharpened stakes shot volleys into French knights, who sank into the mud in heavy armour, crowded together and could not use weapons. Lightly armed archers then killed them with mallets and daggers.
atrocities: Fearing an attack from behind while holding many prisoners, Henry ordered the killing of French prisoners — a breach of the code of chivalry, since prisoners were valuable for ransom. Many English knights refused, so archers did it.
reshaped: Henry V conquered Normandy and was recognised as heir to the French throne by the Treaty of Troyes (1420), though France later recovered under Joan of Arc.
connections: Hundred Years' War; Normans and Plantagenets; William Shakespeare; Joan of Arc

name: The Black Dinner
sides: Scottish royal regents vs the Douglas family
commanders: Sir William Crichton and Sir Alexander Livingston vs William, 6th Earl of Douglas
casualties: The 16-year-old earl and his younger brother executed
summary: The young Earl of Douglas was invited to dine with the 10-year-old King James II and then murdered — a famous betrayal of hospitality that inspired the 'Red Wedding' in Game of Thrones.
betrayal: Legend says a black bull's head, a symbol of death, was placed on the table at the end of the meal; the Douglas boys were dragged out, given a mock trial and beheaded in the castle courtyard despite the young king's pleas.
atrocities: Breaking guest-right was considered among the worst crimes in Scottish society.
reshaped: The killing broke Douglas power temporarily but fuelled decades of conflict. The 1692 Glencoe Massacre, when government soldiers who had been sheltered by the MacDonalds murdered their hosts, is another example of 'murder under trust'.
connections: Edinburgh Castle

name: Fall of Constantinople (siege)
sides: Ottoman Empire vs Byzantine Empire
commanders: Sultan Mehmed II vs Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos
forces: About 80,000 Ottomans vs about 7,000 defenders
casualties: About 4,000 defenders killed in fighting; thousands of civilians killed; about 30,000 enslaved
summary: Ottoman cannon broke the thousand-year-old Theodosian Walls.
tactics: Mehmed bombarded the walls with giant cannon, dug tunnels (countered by Byzantine miners), and hauled about 70 ships overland on greased logs into the Golden Horn to bypass the great chain across the harbour.
betrayal: The cannon founder Orban, a Hungarian, had first offered his services to the Byzantines, who could not pay him; he went to Mehmed. Legend says a small gate, the Kerkoporta, was left open, letting Ottomans in. Venice and the Pope sent little help.
atrocities: The city was sacked for three days; churches were looted and many civilians killed or enslaved.
reshaped: It ended the Roman Empire, made Istanbul the Ottoman capital, pushed Europe to seek sea routes to Asia, and Greek scholars fleeing to Italy helped fuel the Renaissance.
connections: Fall of Constantinople; Byzantine Empire; Ottoman Empire; Theodosian Walls; Palaiologos dynasty

name: Second Battle of Tarain (battle)
sides: Ghurid Empire vs Chahamanas (Chauhans) and allied Rajput kings
commanders: Muhammad of Ghor vs Prithviraj Chauhan III
forces: Perhaps 120,000 Ghurids vs a larger Rajput army
casualties: Heavy Rajput losses; Prithviraj captured and executed
summary: A year after losing at Tarain, Muhammad of Ghor returned and defeated Prithviraj, opening north India to the Delhi Sultanate.
tactics: Ghor used fast mounted archers in units that harassed the Rajput army from all sides, pretended to retreat to break its formation, then charged with heavy cavalry when the Rajputs were exhausted.
betrayal: Later legends claim Jaichand of Kannauj, Prithviraj's rival, did not help him, or even invited Ghor; historians consider this unproven, but the disunity of Rajput kings was real.
atrocities: Ajmer was sacked after the battle.
reshaped: Ghor's general Qutb ud-Din Aibak took Delhi, and in 1206 founded the Delhi Sultanate.
connections: Second Battle of Tarain; Prithviraj Chauhan; Delhi Sultanate; Mamluk (Slave) dynasty

name: Siege of Chittorgarh (1568)
sides: Mughal Empire vs Mewar
commanders: Akbar vs Jaimal Rathore and Patta Sisodia (Rana Udai Singh had withdrawn to the hills)
forces: Large Mughal army vs about 8,000 Rajputs
casualties: Most defenders killed; about 30,000 non-combatants massacred
summary: Akbar took Chittor, Mewar's great hill fort, after a four-month siege, the third time the fort fell.
tactics: Mughals dug sabats — covered approach trenches wide enough for horsemen — up to the walls, and mines packed with gunpowder; one mine blew up killing many of their own soldiers. Akbar personally shot the commander Jaimal with a musket.
atrocities: Chittor's women committed jauhar (self-immolation) to avoid capture, and the men went out in a final charge (saka). Angered by the long resistance, Akbar ordered a massacre of about 30,000 people, including peasants who had sheltered in the fort — an act he later seemed to regret, commissioning statues of Jaimal and Patta at Agra.
reshaped: Mewar's resistance continued under Maharana Pratap; Chittor became a symbol of Rajput honour and sacrifice.
connections: Akbar; Mughal Empire; Rajput kingdoms of Mewar (Sisodia); Rana Pratap; Chittorgarh Fort

name: Battle of Plassey (battle)
sides: East India Company vs the Nawab of Bengal and French allies
commanders: Robert Clive vs Siraj ud-Daulah
forces: About 3,000 Company troops vs about 50,000 Nawab's troops
casualties: About 500 of the Nawab's troops; 22 Company troops
summary: A battle won mainly by bribery opened the way to British rule in India.
tactics: Rain soaked the Nawab's gunpowder while Company troops covered theirs with tarpaulins. When the Nawab's cavalry charge failed, his army began to retreat.
betrayal: Clive had secretly agreed to make the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar the new Nawab; Mir Jafar's large contingent did not fight. Bankers Jagat Seth and Omichund also joined the plot — Clive cheated Omichund with a fake treaty. 'Mir Jafar' became a byword for traitor in India.
atrocities: Siraj ud-Daulah was captured and murdered by Mir Jafar's son. Clive received a personal fortune of about £234,000.
reshaped: The Company controlled Bengal's revenue, the start of colonial rule, the drain of wealth, and the 1770 famine.
connections: Battle of Plassey; Robert Clive; East India Company rule; Black Hole of Calcutta

name: Siege of Cawnpore and Bibighar

commanders: Nana Sahib and Tatya Tope vs General Hugh Wheeler
forces: About 900 British, including civilians
casualties: Most British men killed; about 200 women and children murdered at Bibighar
summary: After a three-week siege the British surrendered on a promise of safe passage, which ended in massacre on both sides.
tactics: Rebels besieged Wheeler's weak entrenchment with artillery in scorching heat.
betrayal: Nana Sahib offered safe passage by boat to Allahabad; at Satichaura Ghat firing broke out — who fired first is disputed — and most men were killed. Women and children were held at the Bibighar.
atrocities: As British relief forces approached, the captive women and children were hacked to death and thrown down a well. reshaped: The massacre was used to justify brutal reprisals and racial hatred; the Company was abolished in 1858.

name: Ambush at Cajamarca
sides: Spanish conquistadors vs the Inca emperor's retinue
commanders: Francisco Pizarro vs Atahualpa
forces: 168 Spaniards vs about 5,000–7,000 unarmed or lightly armed Inca attendants (an army of 80,000 camped nearby)
casualties: Thousands of Inca killed; no Spaniards killed
summary: Pizarro captured Atahualpa in a surprise attack disguised as a meeting.
tactics: Spaniards hid in buildings around the town square with cannon and horses. When the friar Vicente de Valverde handed Atahualpa a Bible and he dropped it, Pizarro gave the signal; guns, cavalry and steel blades caused panic in the crowded square.
betrayal: Atahualpa came as a guest invited for a meeting. After capture he paid a ransom of a room filled with gold and two with silver, but Pizarro had him executed by garrotte in 1533 anyway.
atrocities: The massacre of unarmed attendants; the ransom treasure was melted down.
reshaped: It decapitated the Inca state, already weakened by smallpox and civil war, and opened South America to Spanish rule.
connections: Atahualpa; Spanish conquest of the Inca; Inca Empire; Spanish Empire

name: Glencoe Massacre
sides: Government soldiers vs the MacDonalds of Glencoe
commanders: Captain Robert Campbell of Glenlyon
forces: About 120 soldiers
casualties: About 38 MacDonalds killed; others died of exposure
summary: Soldiers who had accepted MacDonald hospitality for two weeks rose before dawn and killed their hosts.
betrayal: The killing of hosts by guests, 'murder under trust', was a crime in Scots law. It was ordered because the chief had been late signing an oath of allegiance to King William III.
atrocities: Men were shot in their beds; women and children fled into a blizzard.
reshaped: An inquiry blamed officials; it fuelled Jacobite resentment.
connections: Glorious Revolution

name: Wounded Knee Massacre
sides: US Army vs Lakota
commanders: Colonel James Forsyth
forces: About 500 soldiers vs about 350 Lakota
casualties: About 250–300 Lakota killed, many women and children
summary: US soldiers killed Lakota men, women and children while disarming their band.
tactics: Soldiers with Hotchkiss guns surrounded the camp.
betrayal: The band was heading to the reservation and had raised a white flag.
atrocities: Victims were buried in a mass grave; 20 soldiers received the Medal of Honor, which Native groups still ask to be rescinded.
reshaped: It marked the end of armed Native American resistance.
connections: Lakota; United States

name: Battle of the Somme
sides: Britain and France vs Germany
commanders: Douglas Haig vs Erich von Falkenhayn
forces: Millions
casualties: Over 1 million killed or wounded; 57,470 British casualties on the first day alone
summary: One of the bloodiest battles in history, fought for a few kilometres of mud.
tactics: A week-long bombardment of 1.5 million shells was meant to destroy German defences, but many shells were duds and Germans sheltered in deep dugouts. British soldiers walked across no-man's-land into machine-gun fire. Tanks were used for the first time in September.
atrocities: Troops from across the empire, including Indian cavalry, died in huge numbers; shell-shocked soldiers were sometimes shot for 'cowardice'.
reshaped: It came to symbolise the futility of trench warfare and shaped how Britain remembers WWI.
connections: World War I; British Empire

name: Gallipoli campaign
sides: Britain, France, Australia, New Zealand, India vs Ottoman Empire

forces: About 500,000 Allied troops
casualties: About 250,000 casualties on each side
summary: An Allied attempt to seize the Dardanelles and knock the Ottomans out of the war failed.

atrocities: Disease killed many; the Armenian genocide began in the Ottoman Empire at the same time.
reshaped: It made Mustafa Kemal a hero and shaped Australian and New Zealand identity (Anzac Day). About 15,000 Indian soldiers served.

name: Nanjing Massacre
sides: Imperial Japanese Army vs Chinese soldiers and civilians
commanders: General Iwane Matsui; Prince Asaka Yasuhiko
casualties: Estimates range from tens of thousands to over 300,000 killed
summary: After capturing China's capital, Japanese troops committed mass murder and rape over six weeks.
betrayal: Chinese soldiers who surrendered were promised safety and then executed.
atrocities: Mass executions, 'killing contests' reported in Japanese newspapers, and an estimated 20,000 rapes. Westerners like John Rabe, a Nazi party member, set up a safety zone that saved about 250,000 people.
reshaped: The Tokyo Tribunal convicted Matsui. Denial by some Japanese nationalists still strains China–Japan relations.
connections: Japanese invasion of China and the Nanjing Massacre; World War II; Unit 731 and the US cover-up

name: Battle of Stalingrad (battle)
sides: Soviet Union vs Germany and allies
commanders: Vasily Chuikov and Georgy Zhukov vs Friedrich Paulus
forces: Over 1 million on each side
casualties: About 2 million killed, wounded or captured
summary: The turning point of the Eastern Front.
tactics: Street fighting in ruins ('Rattenkrieg'); Soviet troops 'hugged' Germans to avoid bombing; Operation Uranus encircled the Sixth Army.
betrayal: Stalin's Order No. 227 ('Not one step back') had blocking detachments shoot retreating Soviet soldiers.
atrocities: Of 91,000 German prisoners, only about 5,000 returned home.
reshaped: Germany lost the initiative in the east.
connections: Battle of Stalingrad; World War II; Joseph Stalin; Adolf Hitler

sides: US Army vs Vietnamese villagers
commanders: Lieutenant William Calley
forces: About 100 soldiers
casualties: 347–504 unarmed civilians killed
summary: US soldiers murdered hundreds of unarmed villagers, mostly women, children and elderly.

atrocities: Mass shootings and rapes. Helicopter pilot Hugh Thompson landed between soldiers and villagers to save survivors.
reshaped: It turned US opinion further against the war; only Calley was convicted, serving three years of house arrest.
connections: Cu Chi tunnels; Cold War; Gulf of Tonkin incident

name: Operation Searchlight and the 1971 genocide

commanders: General Tikka Khan; General A. A. K. Niazi
casualties: Estimates 300,000 to 3 million killed
summary: Pakistan's army launched a crackdown on Bengali nationalists that became genocide.
betrayal: Militias like Razakars and Al-Badr collaborated; intellectuals were rounded up and killed on 14 December 1971.
atrocities: Mass killings, about 200,000–400,000 women raped, and 10 million refugees fled to India.
reshaped: India intervened and Bangladesh was born on 16 December 1971.

name: Battle of Talikota (battle)
sides: Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar) vs Vijayanagara Empire
commanders: Hussain Nizam Shah and allies vs Aliya Rama Raya
forces: Large armies on both sides; Vijayanagara's perhaps larger
casualties: Heavy Vijayanagara losses; Rama Raya beheaded
summary: An alliance of Deccan sultans destroyed Vijayanagara's army, and its capital Hampi was sacked for months.
tactics: The sultans' artillery, using copper coins as grapeshot in some accounts, and mounted archers broke the Vijayanagara lines after an initially successful attack.
betrayal: Rama Raya had played the sultanates against each other for years, pushing them into alliance. During the battle, two Muslim commanders in Vijayanagara service, the Gilani brothers, with tens of thousands of troops, reportedly turned against him at the decisive moment, and Rama Raya was captured and beheaded.
atrocities: The victors looted Hampi for about six months, destroying temples and palaces; the city never recovered.
reshaped: Vijayanagara's power collapsed and the south fragmented into Nayaka states.
connections: Battle of Talikota; Vijayanagara Empire; Bahmani Sultanate; Krishnadevaraya

name: Third Battle of Panipat (battle)
sides: Maratha Empire vs Durrani Afghans and the Rohillas and Nawab of Awadh
commanders: Sadashivrao Bhau vs Ahmad Shah Durrani (Abdali)
forces: About 45,000–60,000 Maratha soldiers plus many pilgrims and camp followers vs about 60,000–80,000
casualties: Perhaps 60,000–70,000 Marathas killed in battle and many more in the slaughter that followed
summary: One of the largest battles of the 18th century crushed Maratha expansion in the north.
tactics: The Marathas, besieged for two months and starving, attacked with French-trained artillery under Ibrahim Gardi; Abdali's swivel guns on camels (zamburaks) and reserve cavalry broke them late in the day after Vishwasrao was killed.
betrayal: Rajput, Jat and Sikh rulers, alienated by Maratha taxes, refused to help; Suraj Mal of Bharatpur left the camp after disagreements. Najib-ud-Daula persuaded Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh to join Abdali.
atrocities: The day after the battle, Afghan troops massacred thousands of prisoners and enslaved women and children; Ibrahim Gardi was tortured to death.
reshaped: The Maratha defeat and Abdali's withdrawal left a power vacuum that the East India Company filled within decades.
connections: Third Battle of Panipat; Maratha Confederacy; Maratha Empire (Bhonsle and Peshwas)

name: Battle of Saraighat
sides: Ahom Kingdom vs Mughal Empire
commanders: Lachit Borphukan vs Raja Ram Singh I
forces: Ahom river fleet vs much larger Mughal navy and army
casualties: Mughal defeat
summary: A naval battle on the Brahmaputra in which the Ahoms stopped the Mughals from conquering Assam.
tactics: Lachit used the narrow river and hills, earthwork forts, and small boats to outmanoeuvre the bigger Mughal ships. Ill, he had himself carried into battle to rally his retreating men.
betrayal: Mughal commanders tried bribing Ahom leaders with a letter to make Lachit appear disloyal; the Ahom king did not believe it.
reshaped: Assam stayed independent of the Mughals; Lachit Divas is celebrated in Assam.
connections: Lachit Borphukan; Ahom kingdom; Mughal Empire

name: Siege of Seringapatam (1799)
sides: East India Company and Hyderabad vs Kingdom of Mysore

forces: About 50,000 Company and allied troops vs about 30,000
casualties: Tipu killed; about 10,000 Mysoreans
summary: The British stormed Tipu Sultan's island capital and killed him at the walls.
tactics: British guns breached the walls across the Kaveri; troops stormed at midday when defenders were resting.
betrayal: Tipu's minister Mir Sadiq is remembered as a traitor who opened the way and withdrew troops; he was killed by Mysore soldiers. Others, like Purnaiya, later served the British.
atrocities: The city was plundered; Tipu's tiger throne and treasures were taken to Britain.
reshaped: Mysore was restored to the Wodeyars as a British subsidiary state, ending a major obstacle to Company rule in the south.
